comments.author: mtset
comments.text:
I don't think this really does much to refute the point of the article, though I think I read your comment (and its context) as an attempt to do so.

TFA gives the example of Deferred, the process of creating which the calls poetic and whose motivation he calls aesthetic. It also solves a problem - partly an aesthetic problem, but partly a practical problem. I think this is one example of the most common case for software, in which it both solves a practical problem and soothes the aesthetic sensibilities of the creator, the commissioner, or both.

TFA also gives the example of copywriting. Copywriting is writing, and novel-writing is writing; similarly, creating ORCA and Nebu required similar skills in both the macro and micro as each other, and similar skills at least in the macro as writing Excel, FL Studio, and Photoshop. That is, on all four quadrants of the code as art × code for art matrix (art code for making art, art code for doing practical things, utilitarian code for making art, utilitarian code for doing practical things), the same process and skills are employed.

The point is that, yes, code mostly exists to solve a problem, but exactly like writing or painting, the output of the same or similar processes is called "art" based entirely on cultural attitudes toward the output and its context.

comments.text:
You're conflating skill with artistry, and quality with art.

Between junk and art there's a whole gray area of things that are competent, well made, but unoriginal and uncreative.

"What is art" is a tough philosophical question, and in the right context even an off-white eggshell office wall can be an artwork, but we also have lots of office walls where neither the creator nor the audience thinks of as an artwork.

Back to code: are Salesforce admin panels art? Are budget Electron apps art? An enterprise timesheet application may symbolise futility and suffering, but that's probably not what the "artist" meant.

comments.author: dcao
comments.text:
It's only art for fellow programmers. Nobody outside of this really cares.


I'd argue the same can be said of any creative discipline! A musician is using creative techniques and including musical references and callbacks that likely only other musicians (and music enthusiasts/critics) will be able to pick up on. A conceptual artist is creating their work within a longer conversation of other conceptual artwork—referencing prior techniques, critiquing past works and artists—that is mostly legible to artists, curators, historians, and critics with specialized knowledge of the field. (Maybe a parallel in programming would be seeing an I/O-bound Rust program rely exclusively on manual io_uring syscalls as a "critique" of async/await.)

In these cases, a layperson might only see the pragmatic function of these works ("this song sounds good" or "the art looks pretty"); but for someone with familiarity with a particular practice, the work can still be understood more profoundly. If anything, I'd argue that this makes programming even more like art in general, since just like in other creative disciplines, appreciating a work beyond a surface level requires understanding the history and practice of the discipline it's a part of :^)

comments.author: roryokane
comments.text:
My own Robot Simulator entry for one of the contests on BadCode.rocks. I fulfilled the prompt of “the worst working implementation to the challenge that [I could] devise” and won an Honorable Mention.

Along the same lines, the better-known FizzBuzzEnterpriseEdition satirically uses a large framework to solve a simple problem.


Quine Relay does something useless but complex in a way that was obviously hard to build.

The winners of the Underhanded C Contest contain hard-to-find bugs that undermine the program’s purpose but look like accidents after they’re found.


More generally, Improv Everywhere’s 2009 Subway Art Gallery demonstrated to me that “art” is a perspective with which one can view any object, so I think it’s never wrong to call something “art”. But I find more artistic value in works that satisfy challenging contraints. The most common source of artistic value in programs is the way their code was optimized to be easily readable and maintainable by a human while still implementing the required behavior.

comments.author: MatejKafka
comments.text:
I think there's an important difference between art, craft, and (for a lack of a better term) "getting stuff done".

Art, to me, is fundamentally about creative expression that is not necessarily driven by a practical purpose (although good art conveys ideas, emotions or values). A recent example of this might by Lyra Rebane's creative abuse of QR codes.

Craft is about cleverly and efficiently solving problems, which can involve bits of art by solving the problems in creative or aesthetically pleasing ways but the fundamental motivation and aim feels different.

I'm not convinced that art is a necessary (or common) part of day-to-day software work and I don't feel like software artists are particularly impacted by AI, unlike craft, where the impact of AI feels significant.
